EDMUNDS | postcode_district = IP32, IP33 | postcode_area = IP | dial_code = 01284 | os_grid_reference = TL855645 | type = [[Town]] and [[civil parish]] }} '''Bury St Edmunds''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|b|ɛr|i|_|s|ə|n|t|_|ˈ|ɛ|d|m|ən|d|z}}), commonly referred to locally as ''Bury,'' is a [[cathedral]] as well as [[market town]] and [[civil parish]] in the [[West Suffolk District|West Suffolk]] district, in the county of [[Suffolk]], England.OS Explorer map 211: Bury St. Edmunds and Stowmarket Scale: {{gaps|1:25|000}}. Publisher:Ordnance Survey – Southampton A2 edition. Publishing Date:2008. {{ISBN|978 0319240519}} The town is best known for [[Bury St Edmunds Abbey]] and [[St Edmundsbury Cathedral]]. Bury is the seat of the [[Diocese of St Edmundsbury and Ipswich]] of the [[Church of England]], with the [[episcopal see]] at [[St Edmundsbury Cathedral]]. The town, originally called Beodericsworth,{{Cite web|title = Magna Carta 800 – Bury St Edmunds|url = http://magnacarta800.org.uk/blogpart3.html|website = magnacarta800.org.uk|access-date = 22 September 2015|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150923061830/http://magnacarta800.org.uk/blogpart3.html|archive-date = 23 September 2015|url-status = dead|df = dmy-all}} was built on a grid pattern by Abbot Baldwin around 1080.{{Cite web|title = Our Bury St. Edmunds|url = http://www.ourburystedmunds.com/bid-home|website = www.ourburystedmunds.com|access-date = 22 September 2015|archive-date = 23 April 2019|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190423211918/http://www.ourburystedmunds.com/bid-home|url-status = live}}{{Cite web|title=St Edmundsbury Local History - St Edmundsbury from 1066 to 1216|url=http://www.stedmundsburychronicle.co.uk/Chronicle/1066-1216.htm|access-date=18 May 2021|website=www.stedmundsburychronicle.co.uk|archive-date=18 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518100205/http://www.stedmundsburychronicle.co.uk/Chronicle/1066-1216.htm|url-status=live}} It is known for brewing and malting ([[Greene King]] brewery){{Cite web|title = Greene King – Beers & breweries – Our breweries – Greene King Brewery|url = http://www.greeneking.co.uk/index.asp?pageid=10|website = www.greeneking.co.uk|access-date = 22 September 2015|archive-date = 11 June 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160611125914/http://www.greeneking.co.uk/index.asp?pageid=10|url-status = live}} and for a [[British Sugar]] processing factory, where Silver Spoon sugar is produced. The town is the cultural and retail centre for West Suffolk and tourism is a major part of the economy. The built up area had a population of 41,280 at the [[2021 United Kingdom census|2021 census]]. ==Etymology== The name ''Bury'' is [[etymological]]ly connected with ''[[borough]]'',{{cite web | last = Dictionary | first = reference | title = Borough | url = http://dictionary.reference.com/browse/Boroughs | access-date = 15 September 2010 | archive-date = 1 September 2010 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100901172709/http://dictionary.reference.com/browse/boroughs | url-status = live }} which has [[cognate]]s in other [[Germanic languages]] such as German {{lang|de|Burg}} 'fortress, castle' and [[Old Norse language|Old Norse]] {{lang|non|borg}} 'wall, castle'; and [[Gothic language|Gothic]] {{lang|got|baurg}} 'city'.{{cite web | last = dorothea | first = david | title = Gothic Lessons: An Introduction | url = http://members.terracom.net/~dorothea/david/gothic/intro.html | access-date = 15 September 2010 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20040109131448/http://members.terracom.net/~dorothea/david/gothic/intro.html | archive-date = 9 January 2004 | df = dmy-all }} They all derive from [[Proto-Germanic language|Proto-Germanic]] {{lang|gem-x-proto|*burgs}} 'fortress'. This in turn derives from the [[Proto-Indo-European language|Proto-Indo-European]] root {{lang|ine-x-proto|bhrgh}} 'fortified elevation', with cognates including [[Welsh language|Welsh]] ''{{lang|cy|bera}}'' 'stack' and [[Sanskrit]] ''{{lang|sa|bhrant}}-'' 'high, elevated building'. In [[Medieval Latin]] it was known as {{lang|la|Burgum Sancti Edmundi}} (also spelled ''Aedmundi'').Memorials of St. Edmund's abbey: Annales Sancti Edmundi. Electio Hugonis abbatis. Epist. Roberti abbatis de Thorneye. La vie Seint Edmund, by Denis Piramus. Electio Symonis abbatis. Processus contra fratres minores, qualiter expulsi erant de villa Sancti Edmundi. Gesta sacristarum. Electio Thomæ abbatis. Deprædatio abbatiæ Sancti Edmundi. Appendix A, B. (1892:266). United Kingdom: H.M. Stationery Office.Monumenta Germaniae historica inde ab anno Christi quingentesimo usque ad annum millesimum et quingentesimum: Scriptorum. (1964:427). Germany: Impensis Bibliopolii Aulici Hahniani. In the [[Anglo-Saxon]] period the town was called ''Bedricesweord''{{cite encyclopedia|last= Blair |first= John |title=Bury St Edmunds (Suffolk)(''Bedricesweord'') |page=80|year=2014|editor1-first= Michael|editor1-last= Lapidge|editor2-first= John|editor2-last= Blair|editor3-first= Simon|editor3-last= Keynes |editor4-first= Donald|editor4-last= Scragg |encyclopedia=The Wiley Blackwell Encyclopedia of Anglo-Saxon England|edition=2nd| publisher= Wiley Blackwell |location=Chichester, West Sussex |isbn=978-0-470-65632-7}} or ''Bedericesworth''.{{cite book| last=Keynes |first=Simon |chapter=The Burial of King Æthelred the Unready at St Paul's|page=138 |title=The English and their Legacy, 900-1200: Essays in Honour of Ann Williams|editor-first=David|editor-last=Roffe |publisher=The Boydell Press |location =Woodbridge, UK |year=2012|isbn=978-1-84383-794-7}} The second section of the name refers to [[Edmund the Martyr|Edmund]], King of the [[Kingdom of the East Angles|East Angles]], called Edmund the Martyr, who was killed by the [[Great Heathen Army|Vikings]] in the year 869. He became venerated as a saint and a martyr, and his shrine made Bury St Edmunds an important place of pilgrimage. The formal name of the diocese is "St Edmundsbury", and the town is colloquially known as Bury. ==History== [[File:Arms of Bury.jpg|thumb|alt=medieval arms of Bury |Illumination of the [[Coat of arms|arms]] of Bury St Edmunds ([[British Library]])]] An archaeological study in the 2010s on the outskirts of Bury St Edmunds uncovered evidence of Bronze Age activity in the area. The dig also uncovered [[Ancient Rome|Roman]] coins from the first and second centuries.{{cite news|url=http://www.eadt.co.uk/news/prehistoric-remains-uncovered-by-archaeologists-in-bury-st-edmunds-1-5302606|title=Prehistoric remains uncovered by archaeologists in Bury St Edmunds|work=East Anglian Daily Times|date=30 November 2017|access-date=9 February 2018|archive-date=9 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180209182328/http://www.eadt.co.uk/news/prehistoric-remains-uncovered-by-archaeologists-in-bury-st-edmunds-1-5302606|url-status=live}} Samuel Lewis, writing in 1848, notes the earlier discovery of Roman antiquities, and as with several other writers connects Bury St Edmunds with ''Villa Faustini'' or ''Villa Faustina'', although the location of this Roman site is also discussed by [[Edmund Gillingwater|E. Gillingwater]] (1804), who notes the lack of evidence for it being here.{{cite book|section=Burton-upon-Trent – Bushey|title=A Topographical Dictionary of England|editor=Samuel Lewis|location=London|year=1848|pages=452–460|via=British History Online|url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/topographical-dict/england/pp452-460|access-date=9 February 2018|archive-date=9 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180209182451/http://www.british-history.ac.uk/topographical-dict/england/pp452-460|url-status=live}}{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Oj8QAAAAYAAJ|title=A Guide to the Town, Abbey and Antiquities of Bury St. Edmunds…|author=J. Deck|year=1821|page=2|access-date=9 February 2018}}{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bG1HAAAAYAAJ|title=An Historical and Descriptive Account of St. Edmund's Bury, in the County of Suffolk…|author=Edmund Gillingwater|publisher=J. Rackham|year=1804|pages=3–6|access-date=9 February 2018}} The town was one of the royal boroughs of the [[Saxons]]. [[Sigeberht of East Anglia|Sigebert]], king of the [[Kingdom of the East Angles|East Angles]], founded [[Beodricesworth monastery]] here about 633, which in 924{{cite book |last1=Young |first1=Francis |title=Edmund: In Search of England's Lost King |date=2018 |publisher=Bloomsbury |location=London |isbn=978-17867-3-361-0 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wBOMDwAAQBAJ |p=75}} became the burial place of King Edmund the Martyr, who was slain by the [[Danes (Germanic tribe)|Danes]] in 869, and owed most of its early celebrity to the reputed miracles performed at the shrine of the martyr king. The town grew around [[Bury St Edmunds Abbey]], a site of [[pilgrimage]]. In 942 or 945, King [[Edmund I]] had granted to the [[abbot]] and [[convent]] jurisdiction over the whole town, free from all secular services, and [[Canute the Great|Canute]] in 1020 freed it from episcopal control. Later, [[Edward the Confessor]] made the abbot lord of the franchise. The older monastery was destroyed and, the secular priests having been expelled, a new [[Benedictine]] abbey was built.{{cite book|title=Encyclopædia Britannica Eleventh Edition|volume=4|page=868}} Count [[Alan Rufus]] is said to have been interred at Bury St Edmunds Abbey in 1093. In the 12th and 13th centuries the head of the [[de Hastings family]], who held the [[Lordship of the Manor]] of [[Ashill in Norfolk]], was hereditary [[Steward (office)|Steward]] of this abbey.Richardson, Douglas, ''Magna Carta Ancestry'', Baltimore, Md., 2005, p.297.[[File:Moyses Hall Bury St Edmunds early view.jpg|thumb|left|Early view of [[Moyse's Hall]], today Moyse's Hall Museum]] The town was for a time the home of a thriving Jewish community, and it is likely, although not certain, that [[Moyse's Hall]] belonged to a Jewish merchant.{{cite journal |last1=Samuel |first1=Edgar R. |title=Was Moyse's Hall, Bury St. Edmunds, a Jew's House? |journal=Transactions & Miscellanies |date=1973 |volume=25 |pages=43–47 |publisher=Jewish Historical Society of England|jstor=29778836}} On 18 March 1190, two days after the more well-known massacre of Jews at [[York Castle|Clifford Tower]] in [[York]], the people of Bury St Edmunds massacred 57 Jews.Hillaby, Joe. "Jewish Colonisation in the Twelfth Century," in The Jews in Medieval Britain: Historical, Literary, and Archaeological Perspectives, ed. Patricia Skinner (Woodbridge, Suffolk: Boydell Press, 2003), p. 31.Roth, Cecil. A History of the Jews in England (Oxford: Clarendon, 1978). Later that year, [[Samson of Tottington|Abbot Samson]] successfully petitioned [[King Richard I]] for permission to evict the town's remaining Jewish inhabitants "on the grounds that everything in the town... belonged by right to St Edmund: therefore, either the Jews should be St Edmund's men or they should be banished from the town."Jocelin of Brakelond, Chronicle of the Abbey of Bury St Edmunds, trans. Diana Greenway and Jane Sayers (Oxford: Oxford Univ. Press, 1989) This expulsion predates the [[Edict of Expulsion]] by 100 years. In 1198, a fire burned the shrine of St Edmund, leading to the inspection of his corpse by [[Samson of Tottington|Abbot Samson]] and the translation of St Edmund's body to a new location in the [[Bury St Edmunds Abbey|abbey]]. The town is associated with [[Magna Carta]]. In 1214 the [[baron#Barons in the United Kingdom and the Commonwealth|barons of England]] are believed to have met in the abbey church and sworn to force [[John of England|King John]] to accept the [[Charter of Liberties]], the document which influenced the creation of Magna Carta, a copy of which was displayed in the town's cathedral during the 2014 celebrations. By various grants from the abbots, the town gradually attained the rank of a [[borough]]. [[Henry III of England|Henry III]] in 1235 granted to the abbot two annual fairs, one in December and the other the great [[St Matthew]]'s fair, which was abolished by the [[Fairs Act of 1871]]. In 1327, the Great Riot occurred, in which the local populace led an armed revolt against the abbey.{{cite book |title= The Book of Bury St Edmunds |last= Statham|first= Margaret|year= 1988|publisher= Barracuda Books|location= Buckingham, England|isbn= 0-86023-405-3|pages= 12–13}} The riot destroyed the main gate, and a new, fortified gate was built in its stead. On 11 April 1608 a ''great fire'' broke out in Eastgate Street, which resulted in 160 dwellings and 400 outhouses being destroyed. [[File:Warren's map of Bury St Edmunds Suffolk.jpg|thumb|[[Thomas Warren]]'s map of Bury St Edmunds, 1776]] The town developed into a flourishing cloth-making town, with a large [[wool]]len trade, by the 14th century. In 1405 [[Henry IV of England|Henry IV]] granted another fair. [[Elizabeth I]] in 1562 confirmed the charters which former kings had granted to the abbots. The reversion of the fairs and two markets on Wednesday and Saturday were granted by James I in fee farm to the corporation. [[James I of England|James I]] in 1606 granted a charter of incorporation with an annual fair in Easter week and a market. James granted further charters in 1608 and 1614, as did [[Charles II of England|Charles II]] in 1668 and 1684. Parliaments were held in the borough in 1272, 1296 and 1446, but the borough was not represented until 1608, when James I conferred on it the privilege of sending two members. The [[Redistribution of Seats Act 1885]] reduced the representation to one. The borough of Bury St Edmunds and the surrounding area, like much of [[East Anglia]], being part of the [[Eastern Association]], supported [[Puritan]] sentiment during the first half of the 17th century. By 1640, several families had departed for the [[Massachusetts Bay Colony]] as part of the wave of emigration that occurred during the [[Great Migration (Puritan)|Great Migration]].Thompson, Roger, ''Mobility & Migration, East Anglian Founders of New England, 1629–1640'', Amherst: [[University of Massachusetts Press]], 1994. Bury's ancient grammar school also educated such notables as the puritan theologian [[Richard Sibbes]], master of St Catherine's Hall in [[Cambridge]], antiquary and politician [[Simonds d'Ewes]], and [[John Winthrop the Younger]],Thompson, Roger, ''Mobility & Migration, East Anglian Founders of New England, 1629–1640'', Amherst: [[University of Massachusetts Press]], 1994, 18. who became governor of Connecticut. The town was the setting for [[Bury St. Edmunds witch trials|witch trials]] between 1599 and 1694.[[Wallace Notestein|Notestein, Wallace]] ''A History of Witchcraft in England from 1558 to 1718'', American Historical Association 1911 (reissued 1965) New York Russell & Russell,{{OCLC|223043}} [[File:Abbey gate Bury St Edmunds Abbey.jpg|thumb|left|View of gate, Bury St Edmunds Abbey, c. 1920]] ===Modern history=== The population had reached 12,538 by 1841.''The National Cyclopaedia of Useful Knowledge, Vol.III'', London, John Knight, 1847, p.960 A permanent military presence was established in the town with the completion of the [[King's Road drill hall|Militia Barracks]] in 1857{{cite web|url=https://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/101022574-numbers-37-38-and-39-and-attached-walls-bury-st-edmunds#.Wi1gukpl8dU|title=Numbers 37, 38 and 39 and Attached Walls|publisher=British listed buildings|access-date=10 December 2017|archive-date=11 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171211053234/https://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/101022574-numbers-37-38-and-39-and-attached-walls-bury-st-edmunds#.Wi1gukpl8dU|url-status=live}} and of [[Gibraltar Barracks, Bury St Edmunds|Gibraltar Barracks]] in 1878.{{cite web|url=http://www.s234171324.websitehome.co.uk/saunders/the_suffolks.htm|title=History of the Suffolk Regiment|access-date=18 April 2014|archive-date=19 July 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719095106/http://www.s234171324.websitehome.co.uk/saunders/the_suffolks.htm|url-status=live}} During the [[Second World War]], the [[United States Army Air Forces|USAAF]] used [[Rougham Airfield]] outside the town.{{cite web | work = [[St Edmundsbury (borough)|St Edmundsbury Borough Council]] | title = America in Suffolk | url = http://www.stedmundsbury.gov.uk/sebc/visit/suffolk-america.cfm | access-date = 30 December 2007 | archive-date = 9 November 2007 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071109120512/http://www.stedmundsbury.gov.uk/sebc/visit/suffolk-america.cfm | url-status = live }} On 3 March 1974 a [[Turkish Airlines]] [[McDonnell Douglas DC-10|DC10]] jet [[Turkish Airlines Flight 981|Flight 981]] crashed near Paris killing all 346 people on board. Among the victims were 17 members of [[Bury St Edmunds RUFC|Bury St Edmunds Rugby Football Club]], returning from France.{{cite news | url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/onthisday/hi/dates/stories/march/3/newsid_2514000/2514823.stm | title=On This Day, 3 March – 1974: Turkish jet crashes killing 345 | work=[[BBC News Online]] | access-date=24 July 2008 | date=3 March 1974 | archive-date=7 April 2008 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080407052824/http://news.bbc.co.uk/onthisday/hi/dates/stories/march/3/newsid_2514000/2514823.stm | url-status=live }} ==Notable features== Near the abbey gardens stands Britain's first internally illuminated street sign, the [[Pillar of Salt (road sign)|Pillar of Salt]], which was built in 1935. The sign is at the terminus of the [[A1101 road|A1101]], Great Britain's lowest road which is mostly below sea level. There is a network of tunnels which are evidence of [[chalk]]-workings,{{cite web | publisher = [[English Nature]] | url = http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1003555.pdf | title = The Glen Chalk Caves, Bury St Edmunds | access-date = 22 January 2008 | archive-date = 29 February 2008 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080229174727/http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1003555.pdf | url-status = live }} though there is no evidence of extensive tunnels under the town centre. Some buildings have inter-communicating cellars. Due to their unsafe nature the chalk-workings are not open to the public, although viewing has been granted to individuals. Some have caused [[subsidence]] within living memory, for instance at Jacqueline Close.{{cite web |url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1978/nov/29/housing-subsidence |title=HOUSING SUBSIDENCE |work=[[Hansard|Parliamentary Debates (Hansard)]] |date=29 November 1978 |access-date=12 October 2013 |archive-date=15 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131015060911/http://hansard.millbanksystems.com/commons/1978/nov/29/housing-subsidence |url-status=live }} Among noteworthy buildings is [[St Mary's Church, Bury St Edmunds]], where [[Mary Tudor, Queen of France]] and sister of [[Tudor dynasty|Tudor]] king [[Henry VIII of England|Henry VIII]], was re-buried, six years after her death, having been moved from the abbey after her brother's [[Dissolution of the Monasteries]]. [[Queen Victoria]] had a [[stained glass window]] fitted into the church to commemorate Mary's interment.{{cite web | last = Knott | first = Simon | title = Suffolk Churches | url=http://www.simonknott.co.uk/suffolkchurches/burymary.htm | access-date = 30 December 2007 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071203124850/http://www.simonknott.co.uk/suffolkchurches/burymary.htm |archive-date = 3 December 2007}} [[Moreton Hall (Suffolk)|Moreton Hall]], a [[Listed building|Grade II* listed building]] by [[Robert Adam]], houses the now-closed Moreton Hall Preparatory School.British Listed Buildings. [http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-466967-moreton-hall-school-bury-st-edmunds Moreton Hall School, Bury St Edmund's] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111028063703/http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-466967-moreton-hall-school-bury-st-edmunds |date=28 October 2011 }} (English Heritage Building ID: 466967) [[Bury St Edmunds Guildhall]] dates back to the late 12th century.{{cite web|url=https://www.thepilgrimtrust.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/budget1459.pdf|title=An Appeal for the Guildhall, Bury St Edmunds|publisher=The Pilgrim Trust|access-date=24 August 2019|archive-date=24 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190824220357/https://www.thepilgrimtrust.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/budget1459.pdf|url-status=dead}} Bury St Edmunds has one of the full-time fire stations run by [[Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service]]. Originally located in the Traverse (now the Halifax bank),{{cite web |url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/runninginsuffolk/1107130879/in/pool-50views |title=Old Fire Station Bury St Edmunds Suffolk | Flickr – Photo Sharing! |publisher=Flickr |date=16 March 2007 |access-date=10 January 2014 |archive-date=29 June 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629142010/http://www.flickr.com/photos/runninginsuffolk/1107130879/in/pool-50views |url-status=live }} it moved to Fornham Road in 1953. The Fornham Road site (now Mermaid Close) closed in 1987 and the fire station moved to its current location on Parkway North.{{cite web |url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/40382097@N05/3836748422/ |title=Suffolk F&RS – Bury St Edmunds Fire Station | Flickr – Photo Sharing! |publisher=Flickr |date=20 August 2009 |access-date=10 January 2014 |archive-date=21 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131021110014/http://www.flickr.com/photos/40382097@N05/3836748422/ |url-status=live }} Since March 2015, Bury St Edmunds has been the home town of the London and South East Regional Divorce Unit{{cite web | url=https://www.find-court-tribunal.service.gov.uk/courts/bury-st-edmunds-regional-divorce-centre | title=Bury St Edmunds Regional Divorce Centre - Find a Court or Tribunal - GOV.UK |website= |access-date=17 November 2025}} and the Maintenance Enforcement Business Centre (for issues with maintenance payments outside Greater London).{{cite web | url=https://www.gov.uk/child-maintenance-if-one-parent-lives-abroad/other-partner-lives-abroad | title=Child maintenance if a parent lives abroad |website= |access-date=17 November 2025}}{{cite web | url=https://www.thelawpages.com/magistrates-county-crown-court/Maintenance-Enforcement-Business-Centre-(England)-906.html | title=Maintenance Enforcement Business Centre (England) Contact Details, Email, Cases, Daily & Archive Hearing List Records |website= |access-date=17 November 2025}} The former processes divorce documents from across London and South East England as one of five centralised units covering the United Kingdom. Today there are many active churches in the town. ===Abbey=== {{Main|Bury St Edmunds Abbey}} In the centre of Bury St Edmunds lie the remains of an [[abbey]], surrounded by the abbey gardens. The abbey is a [[shrine]] to [[Edmund the Martyr|Saint Edmund]], the [[Kings of East Anglia|Saxon King of the East Angles]]. The abbey was sacked by the townspeople in the 14th century and then largely destroyed during the 16th century with the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries]], but the town remained prosperous throughout the 17th and 18th centuries, only falling into relative decline with the [[Industrial Revolution]]. === Anglican Churches === Until the building of St John's in 1840, the town had just two parishes, St James's and St Mary's.{{Cite web|title=Suffolk Churches|url=http://www.suffolkchurches.co.uk/buryjohn.html|access-date=30 September 2021|website=www.suffolkchurches.co.uk|archive-date=30 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210930162708/http://www.suffolkchurches.co.uk/buryjohn.html|url-status=live}} The former has now become the cathedral. The town now has seven [[Anglican Communion|Anglican churches]] in six parishes, St Peter's being in the same parish as St Mary's.{{Cite web|title=Parish boundaries|url=http://www.wearechurch.net/admin/parish-boundaries/|access-date=30 September 2021|website=St. Mary's with St. Peter's|archive-date=30 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210930162708/http://www.wearechurch.net/admin/parish-boundaries/|url-status=live}} ====Cathedral==== {{Main|St Edmundsbury Cathedral}} St James' parish church became [[St Edmundsbury Cathedral]] when the [[Diocese of St Edmundsbury and Ipswich]] was formed in 1914. The cathedral was extended with an eastern end in the 1960s. A new Gothic revival cathedral tower was built as part of a Millennium project running from 2000 to 2005. The opening for the tower took place in July 2005, and included a [[brass band]] concert and fireworks. Parts of the cathedral remain uncompleted, including the [[cloisters]]. The tower makes St Edmundsbury the most recently completed Anglican cathedral in the UK, and was constructed using original fabrication techniques by six masons who placed the machine-cut stones individually as they arrived. ====St Mary's Church==== {{Main|St Mary's Church, Bury St Edmunds}} St Mary's Church is the civic church of Bury St Edmunds and the third largest parish church in England. It was part of the abbey complex and originally was one of three large churches in the town (the others being St James, now St Edmundsbury Cathedral, and St Margaret's, now gone). It is renowned for its magnificent [[Hammerbeam roof|hammer-beam]] "angel" roof, and is the final resting place of [[Mary Tudor, Queen of France]], [[Duchess of Suffolk]] and favourite sister of [[Henry VIII]]. St Mary's is also home to the Chapel of the [[Suffolk Regiment|Suffolk]] and [[Royal Anglian Regiment]]s. It has collections of fine art, for example [[Mary Beale]], costume, e.g. [[Charles Frederick Worth]], [[horology]], local and social history, including [[Witchcraft]].{{cite web | work = [[St Edmundsbury (borough)|St Edmundsbury Borough Council]] | title = Moyse's Hall Museum | url = http://www.moyseshall.org/ | access-date = 30 December 2007 | archive-date = 11 September 2012 | archive-url = https://archive.today/20120911031536/http://www.moyseshall.org/ | url-status = live }} It holds an original [[death mask]] of William Corder who was hanged for the infamous 1827 [[Red Barn murder]]. The [[Market Cross, Bury St Edmunds|Market Cross]], today a community space, is a building restored by [[Robert Adam]] in 1780s.{{NHLE|num= 1076930|desc= Market Cross|access-date=29 April 2023}} Between 1972 and 2018 the Market Cross was an art gallery called "Smiths Row", hosting a programme of changing contemporary art and craft exhibitions and events by British and international artists.{{Cite web|date=9 June 2018|title=Smiths Row arts organisation announces its closure|url=https://www.suffolknews.co.uk/bury-st-edmunds/news/smiths-row-arts-organisation-announces-its-closure-9001497/|url-status=live|access-date=10 January 2022|website=Suffolk News|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220111091851/https://www.suffolknews.co.uk/bury-st-edmunds/news/smiths-row-arts-organisation-announces-its-closure-9001497/ |archive-date=11 January 2022 }} The town holds several festivals a year. The largest festival is held in May and includes concerts, plays, dance, and lecturers culminating in fireworks. There was an annual Christmas Fair in the town up until 2019, with food, drink, local crafts and fairground rides available, stretching from the Abbey Gardens to the Arc Shopping Centre. Bury St Edmunds is home to England's oldest Scout group, [[Scouting in Suffolk#Scout Groups|1st Bury St Edmunds (Mayors Own)]]. ===Sport=== The town's main [[association football|football]] club, [[Bury Town F.C.|Bury Town]], is the fourth oldest [[non-league]] team in England. They are members of the [[Isthmian League]] and have played at Ram Meadow since moving from [[Cemetry Road|Kings Road]] in the 1970s.{{Cite web|url=https://www.burytownfc.co.uk/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=1&Itemid=2|title=History of Bury Town Football Club – Founded in 1872|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180123050937/http://www.burytownfc.co.uk/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=1&Itemid=2|archive-date=23 January 2018|url-status=dead}} [[Suffolk County Cricket Club]] play occasional games at the Victory Ground, which is also the home ground of Bury St Edmunds Cricket Club. The cricket club previously played at [[Cemetry Road]]. Bury St Edmunds Rugby Football Club has an extensive history,{{cite web|url=http://www.pitchero.com/clubs/burystedmunds/a/history-8750.html |title=History – Bury St Edmunds RUFC |publisher=Pitchero.com |date=29 April 2013 |access-date=12 October 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131014081713/http://www.pitchero.com/clubs/burystedmunds/a/history-8750.html |archive-date=14 October 2013 }} including the devastating [[Turkish Airlines Flight 981|plane crash]] that killed several members who had attended a [[1974 Five Nations Championship]] match. Eastgate Amateur Boxing club was established in 1981. The club has been headquartered at various locations in and around the town, but are now training in an old World War I gym in Rougham. West Suffolk Swimming Club formed in 1998 from the merger of two local swimming clubs and operates from pools in Bury St Edmunds, Haverhill and Culford. West Suffolk Athletics Club are based at the West Suffolk College sports ground.{{cite web|url=http://www.westsuffolkac.com/index.html |title=West Suffolk Athletics Club |access-date=8 January 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150504062627/http://www.westsuffolkac.com/index.html |archive-date=4 May 2015}} [[Nowton Park]] hosts a parkrun every Saturday morning where runners, joggers and walkers can take part free-of-charge, supported by volunteers.{{cite web |title=Bury St Edmunds parkrun |url=https://www.parkrun.org.uk/burystedmunds/ |website=Bury St Edmunds parkrun |access-date=1 December 2024}} A junior parkrun is held every Sunday morning at Ten Acre Field on the Moreton Hall estate, where 4-14 year olds can participate for free, cheered on by volunteers.{{cite web |title=Bury St Edmunds junior parkrun |url=https://www.parkrun.org.uk/burystedmunds-juniors/ |website=Bury St Edmunds junior parkrun |access-date=1 December 2024}} A friendly running club called Bury St Edmunds Pacers welcomes runners of all abilities to join and holds regular running events.{{cite web |title=Bury St Edmunds Pacers |url=https://www.pacers.org.uk/ |website=Bury St Edmunds Pacers |access-date=1 December 2024}} ===Media=== Local news and television programmes is provided by [[BBC East]] and [[ITV Anglia]]. Television signals are received from the [[Tacolneston transmitting station|Tacolneston]] TV transmitter and the local relay transmitter.{{cite web | url=https://ukfree.tv/transmitters/tv/Bury_St_Edmunds | title=Bury St Edmunds (Suffolk, England) Freeview Light transmitter | date=May 2004 }} The town's local radio stations are [[BBC Radio Suffolk]] on 104.6 FM, [[Heart East]] on 96.4 FM and [[RWSfm 103.3|RWSfm]] on 103.3 FM, a community radio station that broadcast from the town. The local newspapers are the [[East Anglian Daily Times]] and [[Bury Free Press]]. ==Local economy== [[File:Bury St Edmunds, Angel Hotel (23401163280).jpg|thumb|Angel Hotel located on Angel Hill]] [[File:Dickens plaque, Angel Hotel 1.JPG|thumb|220x220px|Dickens plaque at The Angel Hotel.|alt=]] ===Tourism=== The Angel Hotel is a [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] building on Angel Hill. [[Charles Dickens]] stayed there while giving readings in the [[Athenaeum, Bury St Edmunds|Athenaeum]], as mentioned in ''[[The Pickwick Papers]]''. [[Angelina Jolie]] stayed there while filming ''[[Lara Croft: Tomb Raider|Tomb Raider]]''. A [[coaching inn]] has existed on the site since the 15th century.{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2009/mar/29/angel-hotel-bury-st-edmunds|title=Checking in: The Angel Hotel, Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk|author=Joanne O'Connor|work=The Guardian|date=29 March 2009|access-date=7 December 2015|archive-date=8 October 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151008044319/http://www.theguardian.com/travel/2009/mar/29/angel-hotel-bury-st-edmunds|url-status=live}} ===Brewing=== [[Greene King]], is situated in Bury St Edmunds, as is the smaller [[The Old Cannon Brewery|Old Cannon Brewery]]. Just outside the town, on the site of [[RAF Bury St Edmunds]], is Bartrums Brewery, originally based in [[Thurston, Suffolk|Thurston]], and to the north is the Brewshed brewery, located in Ingham. The Greene King pub [[The Nutshell]] is situated in the centre of the town, and is one of several that claim to be Britain's smallest [[Pub|public house]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/legacies/heritage/england/suffolk/article_1.shtml|title=BBC – Legacies – Architectural Heritage – England – Suffolk – Beer in a Nutshell – Article Page 1|website=BBC|access-date=5 April 2018|archive-date=25 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925070036/http://www.bbc.co.uk/legacies/heritage/england/suffolk/article_1.shtml|url-status=live}} The [[Corn Exchange, Bury St Edmunds|Corn Exchange]] ([[Wetherspoons]]) is also located nearby. ===Sugar beet=== Bury's largest landmark is the [[British Sugar plc|British Sugar]] factory near the [[A14 road (Great Britain)|A14]], which processes [[sugar beet]] into refined crystal sugar. It was built in 1925 when the town's MP, [[Walter Guinness, 1st Baron Moyne|Walter Guinness]], was [[Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food|Minister of Agriculture]], and for many of its early years was managed by Martin Neumann, former manager of a sugar beet refinery in [[Šurany]], then part of [[Czechoslovakia]]. Neumann was invited by the British government to oversee the refinement of sugar in Bury St Edmunds and, with his family, immigrated to the United Kingdom. The actor and writer [[Stephen Fry]] is a grandson of Martin Neumann, as recounted in the BBC programme ''[[Who Do You Think You Are? (British TV series)|Who Do You Think You Are?]]'' The refinery processes beet from 1,300 growers. 660 lorry-loads of beet can be accepted each day when beet is being harvested. Not all the beet can be crystallised immediately, and some is kept in solution in holding tanks until late spring and early summer, when the plant has spare crystallising capacity. The sugar is sold under the [[British Sugar|Silver Spoon]] name (the other major British brand, [[Tate & Lyle]], is made from imported [[sugar cane]]). By-products include molassed sugar beet feed for cattle and LimeX70, a soil improver. The factory has its own power station,[http://www.cheng.cam.ac.uk/exemplarch2002/mcp21/backimgs.html Industrial-scale evaporators] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080926053124/http://www.cheng.cam.ac.uk/exemplarch2002/mcp21/backimgs.html |date=26 September 2008 }} Chemical Engineering Department, University of Cambridge which powers around 110,000 homes. A smell of burnt starch from the plant is noticeable on some days.{{cite web|url=http://www.englishtowns.net/bury-st-edmunds/|title=Bury St Edmunds|access-date=7 December 2015|archive-date=23 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160323191436/http://www.englishtowns.net/bury-st-edmunds/|url-status=live}} ==Listed buildings== {{main|Listed buildings in Bury St Edmunds (western part)}} {{main|Listed buildings in Bury St Edmunds (eastern part)}} ==Governance== [[File:Entrance porch to Bury St Edmunds Guildhall.jpg|thumb|[[Bury St Edmunds Guildhall|The Guildhall]]]] There are three tiers of local government covering Bury St Edmunds, at [[Parish council (England)|parish]] (town), [[non-metropolitan district|district]], and [[non-metropolitan county|county]] level: Bury St Edmunds Town Council, [[West Suffolk Council]] and [[Suffolk County Council]]. The town council meets at [[Bury St Edmunds Guildhall]], parts of which date back to the 13th century,{{NHLE|desc=The Guildhall and attached railings|num=1363726|grade=I}} and has its offices in an adjoining building at 79 Whiting Street.{{cite web |title=Council and Committee Meetings |url=https://www.burystedmunds-tc.gov.uk/agendas-minutes-2025 |website=Bury St Edmunds Town Council |access-date=14 May 2025}} [[File:West Suffolk House - geograph.org.uk - 1724161.jpg|thumb|West Suffolk House]] West Suffolk Council is also based in the town, at West Suffolk House on Western Way, which was built in 2009 and also includes an area office for the county council.{{cite web |last1=Bunn |first1=Roderic |title=West Suffolk House |url=https://www.usablebuildings.co.uk/UsableBuildings/Unprotected/LCBPWestSuffolkHouse.pdf |website=Usable Buildings |access-date=4 July 2023}}{{cite web |title=Contact us |url=https://www.westsuffolk.gov.uk/contact-us.cfm |website=West Suffolk Council |access-date=17 May 2025}}{{cite web |title=Suffolk County Council offices |url=https://www.suffolk.gov.uk/about/how-to-find-us |website=Suffolk County Council |access-date=17 May 2025}} For national elections, the town forms part of the [[Bury St Edmunds and Stowmarket (UK Parliament constituency)|Bury St Edmunds and Stowmarket]] constituency.{{cite web |title=Election Maps |url=https://www.ordnancesurvey.co.uk/election-maps/gb/ |publisher=Ordnance Survey |access-date=17 May 2025}} The current [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|MP]] is [[Peter Prinsley]] of the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]], who was first elected in the [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024 general election]].{{cite news |title=Bury St Edmunds and Stowmarket - General Election Results 2024 |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/election/2024/uk/constituencies/E14001146 |access-date=21 July 2024}} ===Administrative history=== Bury St Edmunds was an [[ancient borough]]. It is known to have been granted a [[municipal charter]] by [[Henry I of England|Henry I]] (reigned 1100–1135), which has since been lost. The borough was controlled by the abbey until its dissolution in 1539. [[James VI and I|James I]] issued a new charter in 1606, which confirmed Bury's ancient rights and incorporated it under a new constitution. The borough covered the two [[ancient parish]]es of St James and St Mary.{{cite book |title=Report of the Commissioners appointed to inquire into the Municipal Corporations in England and Wales: Appendix 4 |date=1835 |page=2171 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MHBTAAAAcAAJ&dq=edmund&pg=PA2171 |access-date=17 May 2025}} [[File:Register Office, Bury St Edmunds.jpg|thumb|Register Office, 7 Angel Hill; built 1935 as Borough Offices]] The borough was reformed to become a [[municipal borough]] in 1836 under the [[Municipal Corporations Act 1835]], which standardised how most boroughs operated across the country.{{cite book |title=Municipal Corporations Act |date=1835 |page=456 |url=https://archive.org/details/statutesunitedk35britgoog/page/456/mode/2up |access-date=17 May 2025}} Until 30 September 1895 the borough contained the parishes of St James and St Mary when the 2 parishes were merged to form a single Bury St Edmunds parish. The borough was enlarged in 1935 to take in areas from the neighbouring parishes of [[Fornham All Saints]] and [[Westley, Suffolk|Westley]].{{cite web |title=Bury St Edmunds Civil Parish |url=https://visionofbritain.org.uk/unit/10251552#tab02 |website=A Vision of Britain through Time |publisher=GB Historical GIS / University of Portsmouth |access-date=17 May 2025}}{{cite web |title=Bury St Edmunds Municipal Borough |url=https://visionofbritain.org.uk/unit/10153128#tab02 |website=A Vision of Britain through Time |publisher=GB Historical GIS / University of Portsmouth |access-date=17 May 2025}} The borough council historically met at the Guildhall. It moved its offices to a new building called Borough Offices at 7 Angel Hill in 1935. Council meetings continued to be held at the Guildhall until 1966, when a new council chamber was built in an extension to the Borough Offices.{{cite news |title=£100,000 Offices: Foundation stone laying ceremony |url=https://www.findmypast.co.uk/image-viewer?issue=BL%2F0000762%2F19660218&page=6 |access-date=14 May 2025 |work=Bury Free Press |date=18 February 1966 |page=6}} When elected county councils were established in 1889, the old western [[quarter sessions]] division of Suffolk was made the [[administrative county]] of [[West Suffolk (county)|West Suffolk]].{{cite news |title=Parliamentary Intelligence: The Local Government Bill in the House of Lords |work=The Times |date=7 August 1888 |location=London |page=7}}{{cite legislation UK|type=act|act=Local Government Act 1888|year=1888|chapter=41|access-date=2 January 2024}} [[West Suffolk County Council]] was based in Bury, meeting at the town's courthouse, [[Shire Hall Complex, Bury St Edmunds|Shire Hall]], which had been built around 1750.{{NHLE|desc=Old Shire Hall and Magistrates Court|num=1460009|grade=II}}{{cite book |title=Municipal Year Book |date=1966 |publisher=Municipal Journal |page=791}} The borough of Bury St Edmunds, the parish of Bury St Edmunds and administrative county of West Suffolk were abolished on 1 April 1974 under the [[Local Government Act 1972]]. Bury became part of the new [[Borough of St Edmundsbury]], which covered the town and surrounding rural areas. The county-wide [[Suffolk County Council]] was created at the same time.{{cite legislation UK|type=si|si=The English Non-metropolitan Districts (Definition) Order 1972|year=1972|number=2039|access-date=3 March 2023}}{{cite legislation UK|type=si|si=The English Non-metropolitan Districts (Names) Order 1973|year=1973|number=551|access-date=3 March 2023}} St Edmundsbury Borough Council was based in the town, initially using various buildings inherited from its predecessors including the Borough Offices on Angel Hill. In 2009, it consolidated its offices at [[West Suffolk House]], sharing the building with the county council. No [[successor parish]] was created for the area of the abolished municipal borough at the time of the 1974 reforms, and so it became an [[unparished area]]. A new [[civil parish]] of Bury St Edmunds was created on 1 April 2003 which also took in the area of [[Hardwick, Suffolk|Hardwick]] parish that had been abolished in 1988 and had also become unparished.{{cite web|url=https://www.ukbmd.org.uk/reg/districts/bury%20st%20edmunds.html|title=Bury St Edmunds Registration District|publisher=UKBMD|access-date=3 October 2025}} The parish council The town has four [[secondary school]]s: [[Bury St Edmunds County High School]], [[King Edward VI School, Bury St Edmunds|King Edward VI School]], [[St Benedict's Catholic School]] and Sybil Andrews Academy.{{cite web|url=http://www.standards.dfes.gov.uk/trainingschools/schools_directory/?view=get&school=718633&t=1190734444|title=Directory of Training Schools|access-date=25 March 2008}}{{dead link|date=July 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} In 2019 the town's first [[Sixth form college|Sixth Form College]], Abbeygate Sixth Form College, opened. It is located on Beeton's Way. Upon its opening, King Edward VI School closed its Sixth Form provision.{{Cite web |title=Abbeygate Sixth Form College - GOV.UK |url=https://get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Establishments/Establishment/Details/147063 |access-date=20 February 2023 |website=get-information-schools.service.gov.uk |language=en |archive-date=20 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230220184843/https://get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Establishments/Establishment/Details/147063 |url-status=live }} The closest [[Public school (UK)|public school]] (for a period post-war, a [[Direct grant grammar school]]) to the town is [[Culford School]], located just north of the town in the village of [[Culford]]. The town has one independent preparatory school, South Lee School. The former [[Moreton Hall, Bury St Edmunds|Moreton Hall Preparatory School]] closed in 2020.{{Cite web|last=Barnett|first=Sophie|date=22 April 2020|title=Prep school to close for good after coronavirus 'unravels plans for growth'|url=https://www.eadt.co.uk/news/moreton-hall-prep-school-in-bury-st-edmunds-closes-due-2666908|access-date=9 April 2021|website=East Anglian Daily town's largest [[further education]] provider is [[West Suffolk College]], with over 10,000 students studying with the college every year.{{Cite web|url=http://www.westsuffolkcollege.ac.uk/about-us/about-us/key-facts.aspx|title=Key facts {{!}} News and Events{{!}} West Suffolk following a £7m government grant to help pay for an £8m energy, engineering and manufacturing teaching centre.{{Cite web|url=http://www.westsuffolkcollege.ac.uk/news-and-events/latest-news/559/Energy-engineering-and-manufacturing-skills-get-7million-boost-at-West-Suffolk-College|title=Latest news {{!}} News and February 2017|url-status=dead}} From 2015, students have been able to study foundation and undergraduate degrees at the [[University of Suffolk|University of Suffolk at West Suffolk College]].{{Cite September 2015|archive-date=14 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150414073708/http://www.westsuffolkcollege.ac.uk/about-us/about-us/key-facts.aspx|url-status=live}} ==Transport== [[Bury St Edmunds railway station]] serves the town, operated by [[Greater Anglia (train operating company)|Greater Anglia]], on the [[Ipswich to Ely Line]]. Trains run seven days a week, every two hours to Peterborough and hourly to [[Ipswich railway station|Ipswich]] and [[Cambridge railway station|Cambridge]]. Trains from [[Peterborough railway station|Peterborough]] continue to Ipswich after Bury St Edmunds. Onward train connections from [[Cambridge railway station|Cambridge]] link with [[London King's Cross railway station|London King's Cross]], [[Liverpool Street station|London Liverpool Street]] and [[Stansted Airport railway station|Stansted Airport]], whilst [[Ipswich railway station|Ipswich]] provides connections to Liverpool Street via [[Colchester railway station|Colchester]]. The main interchange for bus and coach services for Bury St Edmunds is the bus and coach station, located on St Andrews Street North in the town centre. Bus services link the town centre with the main residential housing areas of the town. From November 2012 Sunday bus services were introduced over some of these routes. There are regular bus services to the neighbouring towns of [[Brandon, Suffolk|Brandon]], [[Cambridge]], [[Diss, Norfolk|Diss]], [[Haverhill, Suffolk|Haverhill]], [[Ipswich]], [[Mildenhall, Suffolk|Mildenhall]], [[Newmarket, Suffolk|Newmarket]], [[Stowmarket]], [[Sudbury, Suffolk|Sudbury]] and [[Thetford]] and many of the villages in between. Daily [[National Express Coaches|National Express]] coach services between [[Victoria Coach Station]] in London and Bury stop at the town's bus and coach station, as does the cross-country service between [[Clacton-on-Sea]] and [[Liverpool]] which travels via Cambridge, Peterborough, [[Leicester]], [[Nottingham]], [[Sheffield]] and [[Manchester]]. The town is partly bisected by the [[A14 road (England)|A14]] trunk road, running east–west and serving as a major transport corridor between the east coast and the Midlands. There are three junctions serving Bury St Edmunds, numbered 42-44 and denoted west, central and east respectively. ==Twin towns== Bury St Edmunds is [[sister city|twinned]] with: * [[Compiègne]], Oise, [[Picardy (region)|Picardy]], France * [[Huy]], [[Wallonia]], [[Liège (province)|Liège]], Belgium * [[Kevelaer]], North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany * [[Xi'an]], Shaanxi, China == Affiliations == *[[HMS Vengeance (S31)|HMS Vengeance]]: Royal Navy Vanguard Class [[SSBN]]{{cite web|url=http://www.royalnavy.mod.uk/operations-and-support/submarine-service/ballistic-submarines-ssbn/hms-vengeance/ |title=HMS Vengeance : Ballistic Submarines (SSBN) : Submarine Service : Operations and Support : Royal Navy |access-date=15 December 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100107224620/http://www.royalnavy.mod.uk/operations-and-support/submarine-service/ballistic-submarines-ssbn/hms-vengeance/ |archive-date=7 January 2010}} ==Literature== Bury St Edmunds is a location mentioned several times in the short ghost story [[The Ash-tree]] by [[M.R. James]] published in ''[[Ghost Stories of an Antiquary]]'' in 1904. Author [[Norah Lofts]], though born in [[Shipdham]], Norfolk, bases many of her stories in Baildon, a fictionalised Bury St Edmunds, where she was educated and lived.{{Cite news|last=Saltmarsh|first=Abigail|date=23 December 2016|title=A House That Inspired a British Novelist|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/12/23/realestate/a-house-that-inspired-a-british-novelist.html|access-date=9 April 2021|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=12 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200612063039/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/12/23/realestate/a-house-that-inspired-a-british-novelist.html|url-status=live}} ==Arms== {{Infobox COA wide |title=Bury St Edmunds Town Council |escutcheon = Azure three open crowns Or each transfixed with two arrows in saltire [points downward] Argent. |crest = On a wreath of the colours a wolf sejant Proper holding a king's head couped at the neck of the last crowned Or. |mantling = Gules doubled Argent. |motto = Sacrarium Regis Cunabula Legis (The Shrine Of The King And The Cradle Of The Law){{cite web |url=http://civicheraldry.co.uk/east_of_england.html |title=East of England Region |publisher=Civic Heraldry of England |access-date=10 March 2021 |archive-date=3 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210503163713/http://www.civicheraldry.co.uk/east_of_england.html |url-status=live }} |notes = Granted 29 November 1606}} ==See also== *[[Cloisters Cross|Bury St Edmunds Cross]] == Notes == {{notelist|30em}} ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== {{EB1911 poster|Bury St Edmunds}} {{Commons category}} *{{wikivoyage inline|Bury St Edmunds}} *[http://www.stedmundsbury.gov.uk St Edmundsbury Council] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191229215041/http://www.stedmundsbury.gov.uk/ |date=29 December 2019 }} *[http://www.burypastandpresent.org.uk Bury St Edmunds Past and Present Society] *[https://www.welovebse.com/jewels/ We Love Bury St Edmunds! 1416223.title: Orford Ness
1416223.extract: Orford Ness is a cuspate foreland shingle spit on the Suffolk coast in Great Britain, linked to the mainland at Aldeburgh and stretching along the coast to Orford and down to North Weir Point, opposite Shingle Street. It is divided from the mainland by the River Alde, and was formed by longshore drift along the coast. The material of the spit comes from places further north, such as Dunwich. Near the middle point of its length, at the foreland point or "Ness", once stood Orfordness Lighthouse, demolished in summer 2020 owing to the encroaching sea. In the name of the lighthouse (and the radio transmitting station – see below), "Orfordness" is written as one word.

main.*:
{{Short description|Coastal shingle spit in Suffolk, England}} {{EngvarB|date=June 2017}} {{Use dmy dates|date=June 2017}} {{for|the place in Australia|Apudthama National Park}} {{Infobox Military Test Site |name=Orford Ness |image=Looking towards Orford Ness from Orford castle - geograph.org.uk - 1755769.jpg |caption=Looking towards Orford Ness from Orford castle | map_type =Suffolk | map_caption = Shown in Suffolk | type= National Nature Reserve, Site of Special Scientific Interest, internationally important site for nature conservation, former military test site | coordinates= {{coord|52|04|53|N|01|33|31|E}} | nearest_town= [[Orford, Suffolk]] | operator= [[Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Defence]], [[Atomic Weapons Establishment|Atomic Weapons Research Establishment]], [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty]] | status=Inactive | dates= 1913 – early 1983 }} '''Orford Ness''' is a [[cuspate foreland]] [[spit (landform)|shingle spit]] on the [[Suffolk]] coast in Great Britain, linked to the mainland at [[Aldeburgh]] and stretching along the coast to [[Orford, Suffolk|Orford]] and down to North Weir Point, opposite [[Shingle Street]]. It is divided from the mainland by the [[River Alde]], and was formed by [[longshore drift]] along the coast. The material of the spit comes from places further north, such as [[Dunwich]]. Near the middle point of its length, at the foreland point or "Ness", once stood [[Orfordness Lighthouse]],{{cite web | title=Orfordness Lighthouse | url=http://www.trinityhouse.co.uk/interactive/gallery/orfordness.html | publisher=Trinity House | access-date=11 October 2007 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071031032453/http://www.trinityhouse.co.uk/interactive/gallery/orfordness.html | archive-date=31 October 2007 | url-status=dead | df=dmy-all }} demolished in summer 2020 owing to the encroaching sea.{{cite web|title=Orfordness Lighthouse: Historic Suffolk landmark reduced to rubble|url= https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-suffolk-53735247|date= 11 August 2020|publisher=BBC}} In the name of the lighthouse (and the radio transmitting station – see below), "Orfordness" is written as one word. ==Description== Orford Ness is an internationally important site for nature conservation. It contains a significant portion of the European reserve of vegetated shingle habitat,{{cite web | title=Coastal Vegetated Shingle | url=http://www.ukbap.org.uk/ukplans.aspx?ID=29 | publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee | access-date=2 June 2008 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080307110538/http://www.ukbap.org.uk/ukplans.aspx?ID=29 | archive-date=7 March 2008 | url-status=dead | df=dmy-all }} which is internationally scarce, highly fragile, and very easily damaged. Together with [[Havergate Island]] the site is a designated [[National Nature Reserve]]{{cite web | title=Orfordness-Havergate NNR | url=http://www.english-nature.org.uk/special/nnr/nnr_details.asp?nnr_name=&C=38&Habitat=0&natural_area=&local_team=0&spotlight_reserve=0&X=&NNR_ID=124 | publisher=Natural England}} and forms part of: the Alde-Ore Estuary [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSI);{{cite web | title=Alde-Ore Estuary SSSI | url=http://www.english-nature.org.uk/special/sssi/sssi_details.cfm?sssi_id=1003208 | publisher=Natural England}} the Alde, Ore & Butley Estuaries{{cite web | title=Alde, Ore and Butley Estuaries SAC | url=http://www.jncc.gov.uk/protectedsites/sacselection/sac.asp?EUCode=UK0030076 | publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee}} and the Orfordness-Shingle Street{{cite web | title=Orfordness-Shingle Street SAC | url=http://www.jncc.gov.uk/protectedsites/sacselection/sac.asp?EUCode=UK0014780 | publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee}} [[Special Area of Conservation]] (SAC); the Alde-Ore Estuary [[Special Protection Area]] (SPA);{{cite web | title=Alde-Ore Estuary SPA | url=http://www.jncc.gov.uk/page-1400 | publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee}} the Alde-Ore Estuary [[Ramsar Convention|Ramsar Site]] site;{{cite web | title=Alde-Ore Estuary Ramsar| url=http://www.jncc.gov.uk/page-1389 | publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee}} the Suffolk Coasts and Heaths [[Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]] (AONB);{{cite web | title=Suffolk Coasts and Heaths AONB | url=http://www.countryside.gov.uk/LAR/Landscape/DL/aonbs/aonb_suffolkch.asp | publisher=Natural England | access-date=2 June 2008 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080724204334/http://www.countryside.gov.uk/LAR/Landscape/DL/aonbs/aonb_suffolkch.asp | archive-date=24 July 2008 | url-status=dead | df=dmy-all }} and the Suffolk Heritage Coast.{{cite web | title=Suffolk Heritage Coast | url=http://www.countryside.gov.uk/LAR/Landscape/DL/heritage_coasts/suffolkhc.asp | publisher=Natural England | access-date=2 June 2008 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080908104154/http://www.countryside.gov.uk/LAR/Landscape/DL/heritage_coasts/suffolkhc.asp | archive-date=8 September 2008 | url-status=dead | df=dmy-all }} It is also listed as of national importance in the [[Geological Conservation Review]] (GC),{{cite web | title=Orfordness and Shingle Street GCR | url=http://www.jncc.gov.uk/default.aspx?page=4174&gcr=1758 | publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee}} as a grade 1 site in the [[Nature Conservation Review]].{{cite book | title=A Nature Conservation Review: the Selection of Sites of Biological National Importance to Nature Conservation in Britain. 2 Volumes. | first=D. A. | last=Ratcliffe | publisher=Cambridge University Press | year=1977 }} (NCR) and qualifies for the DEFRA Environmentally Sensitive Area (ESA) scheme.{{cite web|title=Suffolk River Valleys ESA |url=http://www.defra.gov.uk/erdp/schemes/esas/stage2/suffolkrivers.htm |publisher=Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030623225616/http://www.defra.gov.uk/erdp/schemes/esas/stage2/suffolkrivers.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=23 June 2003 }} ==History== [[File:Appleton-Alb345b.1Cropped.jpg|thumb|left|Orford Ness is the peninsula left of and below the river (River Alde) in this 1588 map]] The peninsula was formerly administered by the [[Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Defence]], which conducted secret military tests during both world wars and the [[Cold War]]. The site was selected as the location for the [[Orfordness Beacon]], one of the earliest experiments in long-range [[radio navigation]]. The Beacon was set up in 1929 and used in the pre-war era. In the 1930s Orford Ness was the site of the first purpose-built experiments on the defence system that would later be known as radar. Having proved the technology on Orford Ness, [[Robert Watson-Watt]] and his team moved to nearby [[Bawdsey Manor]] and developed the [[Chain Home]] radar system in time for its vital role in the Battle of Britain.{{cite web |url=http://www.visit-orford.co.uk/articles/the-birthplace-of-radar-orford-ness-greatest-secret |title=The Birthplace of Radar - Orford Ness' Greatest Secret |first=Paddy |last=Heazell |publisher=Visit Orford |access-date=21 April 2018}} The [[Atomic Weapons Research Establishment]] had a base on the site, used for environmental testing, i.e. testing conducted to determine the functional performance of a component or system under conditions that simulate the real environment in which the component or system is expected to operate. Many of the buildings from this time remain clearly visible from the [[quay]] at Orford, including the distinctive "pagodas".{{cite web |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1416933 |title=Orford Ness: the Atomic Weapons Research Establishment test buildings and associated structures |publisher=Historic England |access-date=21 April 2018}} {{Orford Ness map}} In the late 1960s an experimental Anglo-American military [[over-the-horizon radar]] known as [[Cobra Mist]] was built on the peninsula. It closed in 1973, and in the late 1970s and early 1980s the site and building were re-used for the [[Orfordness transmitting station]]. This powerful [[mediumwave|medium-wave radio]] station – originally owned and run by the [[Foreign and Commonwealth Office|Foreign Office]], then the [[BBC]] and, after privatisation in the 1990s, a series of private companies – was best known for transmitting the [[BBC World Service]] in English around the clock to continental Europe on 648 kHz from September 1982 until March 2011. The following year, the site became disused until [[Radio Caroline]] began broadcasting from it in December 2017.{{cite web |title=The Transmission Gallery - Orford Ness |url=https://tx.mb21.co.uk/gallery/gallerypage.php?txid=1654 |website=tx.mb21.co.uk |access-date=29 November 2025}} Orford Ness is now owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] and is open to the public under the name Orford Ness National Nature Reserve, though access is strictly controlled to protect the fragile habitats and due to a residual danger to the public from the site's former use by the military. Access is available only by the National Trust ferry from Orford Quay on designated open days.{{cite web|author=road |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/orfordness |title=Orford Ness National Nature Reserve |publisher=National Trust |access-date=2018-04-21}} [[Urban exploration|Urban explorers]] have also visited the site.{{Cite web |url=https://www.28dayslater.co.uk/threads/orford-ness-awre-and-cobra-mist-suffolk-october-2018.115056/ |title=Exploration Report - Orford Ness AWRE and Cobra Mist - Suffolk - October 2018 |website=www.28dayslater.co.uk |access-date=29 November 2025}} Rachel Woodward writes:
It is a place of strange contrasts. For the National Trust, its "elemental nature" contrasts with the "inherent dangers" of this place, a "hostile and potentially dangerous site". Military structures – the Bomb Ballistics Building, the Black Beacon, the "pagodas" used for explosive design – have been converted into viewing spots. This is not a celebratory site, however; there is ambivalence and doubt here, with regard to what is being physically and ideologically conserved.{{cite book | title=Military Geographies | first=Rachel | last=Woodward |date=October 2004 | publisher=Blackwell Publishing | isbn=1-4051-2777-5}}{{efn|Note: Woodward states that the testing grounds closed in the early 1990s.}}
Owing to its military history, its stark appearance and the fact that it was closed to the public for many decades, several apocryphal stories have circulated about Orford Ness. The best-known is the suggestion that [[Nazism|Nazi]] troops attempted to invade England and actually disembarked at the tip of the peninsula near [[Shingle Street]], before being repelled with a wall of fire. Official sources denied that any such attempted invasion took place, an assertion confirmed by classified documents released in 1993. More recently, the flashes of the lighthouse were implicated in the [[Rendlesham Forest incident|Rendlesham Forest UFO sightings]] of late December 1980. In 2013, [[Trinity House]] announced that the lighthouse was to be decommissioned as an aid to navigation and marked on UKHO charts as disused.{{Cite web |url=http://www.trinityhouse.co.uk/mariner_info/notice_to_mariners/c/27032013.html |website=www.trinityhouse.co.uk |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130502014703/http://www.trinityhouse.co.uk/mariner_info/notice_to_mariners/c/27032013.html|title=Notice to mariners|archive-date=2 May 2013}} It was demolished in summer 2020. In September 2023, the National Trust employed contractor [[Royal BAM Group|Bam]] (working with [[Historic England]] and [[University College London]]'s [[The Bartlett|Bartlett School]] for Sustainable Construction) to survey the site - in particular, the AWRE Labs 4 and 5, or pagodas - using drones and a dog-like robot named Spot, manufactured by US firm [[Boston Dynamics]]. Concrete decay meant the buildings could not be safely surveyed by human surveyors. National Trust archaeologist Angus Wainwright said the team wanted "to see if it's possible to do a really detailed building survey with no human operator in the building."{{cite news |title=Robot dog surveys nuclear weapons site |url=https://www.theconstructionindex.co.uk/news/view/robot-dog-surveys-nuclear-weapons-site |access-date=11 September 2023 |work=The Construction Index |date=11 September 2023}} File:Ferry,_Orford_Ness_-_geograph.org.uk_-_535535.jpg|View from the Orford Ness dock towards Orford Quay File:The_Radar_Tower,_Orfordness_-_geograph.org.uk_-_287811.jpg|The [[Orfordness Beacon|"Black Beacon" radio navigation tower]] and the lighthouse File:Orfordness_transmitting_station.jpg|Aerial view of the [[Orfordness transmitting station]] File:Orfordness Lighthouse - geograph.org.uk - 2600984.jpg|The lighthouse File:Orford_Ness_pagoda_exterior.jpg|Exterior of two "pagodas" File:Orford_Ness_pagoda_interior.jpg|Interior of a "pagoda" ==Geography== [[File:Orford Ness Map (UK).svg|thumb|right|upright=1.25|Map showing the fluctuating historical extent of Orford Ness]] Orford Ness is Europe's largest vegetated shingle spit.{{cite web | title=The effects of nesting gulls on the shingle vegetation at Orford Ness Suffolk | first=Paul | last=Evans | publisher=School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich | url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-orfordness-guanification_report.pdf | access-date=23 October 2006 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060520211620/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-orfordness-guanification_report.pdf | archive-date=20 May 2006 | url-status=dead | df=dmy-all }}{{efn|The name ''ness'' means 'promontory'. See {{cite book | title=The Northmen in New England, Or, America in the Tenth Century | url=https://archive.org/details/northmeninnewen01smitgoog | first=Joshua | last=Toulmin Smith |author-link=Joshua Toulmin Smith| publisher=Hilliard, Gray, & co | year=1839 | page=[https://archive.org/details/northmeninnewen01smitgoog/page/n220 186]}}}} It is approximately {{convert|10|mi|km}} long,Annex 06: Orfordness in: {{cite web | title=Coastal habitat restoration – towards good practice | year=2003 | publisher=English Nature | url=http://www.english-nature.org.uk/livingwiththesea/project_details/good_practice_guide/shingleCRR/shingleguide/Annexes/Annex06Orfordness/Index.htm}} and the site covers a total area of approximately {{convert|2230|acre|ha}}. Forty percent of this (890 acres) is shingle, 25 percent (556 acres) tidal rivers, mud flats, sand flats, and lagoons, eighteen percent (400 acres) grassland, and fifteen percent (330 acres) salt marsh.{{cite web |date=January 2001 |title=Orfordness – Shingle Street |url=http://www.jncc.gov.uk/ProtectedSites/SACselection/n2kforms/UK0014780.pdf |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee}} The spit formed almost entirely of flint deposited by waves through the process of long-shore drift. The main influence on its formation has been storm waves throwing shingle over the top of the beach crest, where it is protected from ordinary wave action. Over time, this process leads to the formation of stable ridges of fine particles, and swails of coarser shingle. The size and shape of the spit have fluctuated over time (see map). Estimated growth rates range from 64m per year in 1962 to 1967, to 183m per year in 1804 to 1812. Between 1812 and 1821, the total length fluctuated by {{convert|1.8|mi|km}}.{{cite book | title=Geomorphological Processes and Landscape Change: Britain in the Last 1000 Years | first=E. '''Ickworth House''' is a [[English country house|country house]] at [[Ickworth]], near [[Bury St Edmunds]] in [[Suffolk]], England. It is a [[Neoclassical architecture|neoclassical]] building set in parkland. The house was the residence of the [[Marquess of Bristol|Marquesses of Bristol]] until 1998; the house was given to the [[National Trust]] in 1956, but between then and 1998 the marquesses leased the east wing.

==History==
The house, built between 1795 and 1829, was formerly the chief dwelling of an estate owned by the Hervey family, later Marquesses of Bristol, since 1467. The building was the creation of [[Frederick Hervey, 4th Earl of Bristol]] and [[Bishop of Derry]] (known as the Earl-Bishop), who commissioned the Italian architect [[Antonio Asprucci]] to design him a classical villa in the Suffolk countryside. Originally it had been planned as an art gallery but the Earl's collection was seized by [[Napoleon]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=National Trust Book of Scones: 50 Delicious Recipes and Some Curious Crumbs of History|last=Clelland|first=Sarah|publisher=National Trust Books|year=2017|isbn=978-1-909881-93-8|location=London|pages=46}}</ref> The Earl died in 1803, leaving the completion of house to his successor.

In 1956, the house, park, and a large endowment were given to the [[National Trust]] in lieu of [[death duties]]. As part of the handover agreement, a 99-year lease on the 60-room East Wing was given to the [[Marquess of Bristol]]. However, in 1998 the [[John Hervey, 7th Marquess of Bristol|7th Marquess of Bristol]] sold the remaining lease on the East Wing to the National Trust. He was succeeded by his half-brother [[Frederick Hervey, 8th Marquess of Bristol|Frederick William Augustus Hervey, 8th Marquess of Bristol]] (born 19 October 1979). The National Trust refused to sell the remaining lease term back to the 8th Marquess, thereby contravening the Letter of Wishes which states that the head of the family should always be offered whatever accommodation he chooses at Ickworth.{{citation needed|date=February 2025}}

The family's once private East Wing is now run as The Ickworth Hotel on a lease from the National Trust. Apartments, also leased from the Trust, are located in the Dower House in the grounds.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.edp24.co.uk/business/new_owners_for_ickworth_hotel_1_1149959|title=New owners for Ickworth hotel|date=9 December 2011|access-date=23 August 2014|archive-date=27 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140527215652/http://www.edp24.co.uk/business/new_owners_for_ickworth_hotel_1_1149959|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The West Wing at Ickworth House went uncompleted until 2006, when a joint partnership between the National Trust and [[Sodexo|Sodexo Prestige]] led to its renovation and opening as a centre for conferences and events. The first wedding in the property's history took place in 2006.{{citation needed|date=October 2018}}

==Architecture==

[[File:Ickworth House2.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The entrance facade and ionic portico (''9 on plan'').]]
[[File:Ickworth House5.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The West Wing; its interior remained unfinished until 2006]][[File:Ickworth House 2020 Renovation.jpg|thumb|The renovation of the Rotunda, which started in 2019|alt=|300x300px]]

As one of England's more unusual houses, Ickworth has been unflatteringly described as resembling "a huge bulk, newly arrived from another planet" and as "an overgrown folly".<ref name="Jackson-Stopps, p.118">Jackson-Stopps, p.118.</ref> It is now being architecturally reassessed and recognised as the only building in England comparable with the monumental works of [[Étienne-Louis Boullée|Boullée]] and [[Claude Nicolas Ledoux|Ledoux]].<ref name="Jackson-Stopps, p.118" />

The design concept was based on the designs of Italian architect [[Antonio Asprucci]], most noted for his work at the [[Villa Borghese]], which the Bishop-Earl had seen. Asprucci's plans were adapted and the building work overseen by the Irish architects [https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803100440544;jsessionid=FAAFDD663340CBB97FA88AAF93D73AC8 Francis Sandys] and his brother [[Joseph Sandys]].

The façades are of brick covered in stucco; beneath a roof of slate and lead. The central rotunda is {{convert|105|ft|m}}. high with a domed and balustraded roof. the building is entered through the central entrance [[Ionic order|ionic]] pedimented [[portico]].

The rotunda is decorated with pilasters, which on the lower floor are Ionic and Corinthian above. The ground and first floor and the third floor and the balustraded parapet are divided friezes bas-relief.

The rotunda is flanked by segmental single story narrow wings (appearing as a blind arcade) linking, in the [[palladian]] fashion, to two terminating pavilions; these segmental wings are broken at their centre by projecting bays which house the Smoking Room and the Pompeian Room, both later 19th century additions.

Unlike the design of a true Palladian building, the terminating pavilions, rather than minor balancing appendages, are in fact large wings, complementary in weight to the rotunda which becomes their [[corps de logis]]. The East Wing, a small mansion in itself, was designed to be the everyday living quarters of the family (which it remained until 1998), thus permitting the more formal rooms of the rotunda to be reserved for entertaining and display. The west wing, intended as an [[orangery]], sculpture gallery and service rooms remained an unfinished shell until the beginning of the 21st century.  For much of the time it was used as agricultural storage and latterly for playing [[Squash (sport)|squash]] on a court installed by the [[Frederick Hervey, 4th Marquess of Bristol|4th Marquess]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Ickworth |last=Pusey |first=Catharine |publisher=[[The National Trust]] |isbn=978-1-84359-383-6 |year=2011}}</ref>

== Contents ==

The house has paintings by [[Diego Velázquez|Velázquez]], and [[Titian]], as well as a series of 18th-century family portraits by artists such as [[Thomas Gainsborough|Gainsborough]], [[Joshua Reynolds|Reynolds]], [[Vigee-Lebrun]], [[Pompeo Batoni|Batoni]], [[Angelica Kauffman]], [[Allan Ramsay (artist)|Ramsay]], [[Jacob van Loo|van Loo]], and [[William Hogarth|Hogarth]]. In addition, it has a collection of fine [[Georgian era|Georgian]] [[Silver (household)|silver]]. The house also contains very good examples of [[English Regency|Regency]] furniture, [[porcelain]] and 16th century maiolica.  As well, [[Geraldine Hervey, Marchioness of Bristol]] used to collect elaborately decorated fans, and silver fishes.

==Ickworth Church==
{{main|St Mary's Church, Ickworth}}
Most members of the Hervey family, from Thomas Hervey (d. 1467) up to the [[John Augustus Hervey, 7th Marquess of Bristol|7th Marquess of Bristol]] (d. 1999), have been buried at [[St Mary's Church, Ickworth|Ickworth Church]], which is located in the Park, a short walk from the house. The church is [[Norman architecture|Norman]] with some later additions, and possesses a 15th-century wall painting of the [[Gabriel|Angel of the Annunciation]], a 15th-century [[Baptismal font|font]], and roundels of [[Flanders|Flemish]] glass from as early as 14th century, as well as numerous [[marble]] achievements to different members of the Hervey family over the centuries. It remains in the hands of the Hervey family and has recently undergone repairs to make it safe with the help of a grant from [[English Heritage]].

== The Park ==
Ickworth Park covers an area of over {{convert|1800|acres}}.<ref name="lett">{{cite web |url=https://www.eadt.co.uk/news/21321946.7-suffolks-interesting-trees/ |title=7 of Suffolk’s most interesting trees |last=Lett |first=Danielle |publisher=[[East Anglian Daily Times]] |date=20 February 2021 |access-date=26 December 2022}}</ref> The park contains "some of the finest ancient trees in the area."<ref name="secret">{{cite web |url=https://secretsuffolk.com/ickworth/ |title=Ickworth |publisher=/secretsuffolk.com |access-date=26 December 2022 }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> The Tea Party Oak, which is at least 800 years old, is located south of Ickworth Lodge and has a diameter of over {{convert|9|m}}.<ref name="lett"/> It is one of the county's oldest surviving [[oak]] trees. Another tree, in Albana Wood, is about 600 years old.<ref name="secret"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.geograph.org.uk/photo/832151 |title=Tea Party Oak, Ickworth Park |date=4 June 2008 |publisher=geograph.org.uk |access-date=26 December 2022}}</ref>

3002654.title: Bridge Cottage
3002654.extract:
Bridge Cottage is a 16th-century thatched cottage in Flatford, East Bergholt, Suffolk, England. It has been  a National Trust property since 1943 and a Grade II* listed building since 1955. The National Trust market the property under the name "Flatford: Bridge Cottage". The building is timber framed, but this is not evident from the outside as it is rendered.  The II* grading, unusual for an architecturally unremarkable cottage, "reflects the importance of the cottage as part of the Flatford Mill group and its significance in the work of John Constable". 
The property is located in the heart of Dedham Vale, a typical Suffolk rural landscape. It is noted as the location for works by John Constable, and presents an exhibition of his paintings.
The cottage is located just upstream from Flatford Mill which, along with neighbouring Valley Farm and Willy Lott's Cottage, are leased to the Field Studies Council; a group uses them as locations for arts-based courses.
The property provides access to a number of walks along the River Stour.

3701745.title: Theatre Royal, Bury St Edmunds
3701745.extract:
The Theatre Royal, formerly the New Theatre, is a restored Regency theatre in Bury St. Edmunds, Suffolk, England. The building is one of eight Grade I listed theatres in the United Kingdom, and is the only working theatre operated under the auspices of the National Trust. It is considered to be one of the most perfect examples of Regency theatres in Britain.
The theatre presents a diverse programme of drama, music and stand-up comedy. It regularly produces its own work which tours nationally, recent productions include Torben Bett's Invincible in the summer of 2016 and, in early 2017, an adaptation of Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey.
The Theatre Royal is currently a member of the pioneering Black Theatre Live partnership, a consortium of eight UK theatres committed to effecting change nationally for BAME touring through a three-year programme of national touring, structural support and audience development.
